articles.title: This 2-Second Test Can Instantly Tell You If You’re Dehydrated—Especially If You’re Also Exhibiting These Signs
articles.content:
脱水善于伪装成其他问题。你的头痛了，可能会归咎于长时间盯着屏幕；你感到疲惫，可能会怪罪于睡眠不足；站起来时感到晕眩，大脑可能立刻想到更严重的问题：是铁缺乏？低血糖？还是生命垂危？有时候，你真的只是需要多喝水。

然而，虽然很多人认为轻度脱水是普遍现象，但评估脱水并不像表面看起来那么简单。幸运的是，人体会留下一些线索。除了明显的口渴症状外，还有许多容易被忽视的信号。而且，有一个简单的皮肤测试可以在几秒钟内完成，但有一个重要提示：这个测试可以提供有用的信息，但不应该是判断是否脱水的唯一标准。

米切尔·罗斯纳（Mitchell Rosner）博士，一位专门研究液体和电解质失调的肾脏病学家，以及詹姆斯·温格（James Winger）博士，一位研究运动中人体液体管理的运动医学医生，解释了脱水时人体发生的变化以及如何及时发现症状。

当身体失去液体时，必须进行调整以影响循环、温度调节，最终影响器官功能。罗斯纳博士指出，脱水会减少血液容量，降低血压，迫使心脏跳动更快以保持血液循环。失去液体和电解质还会导致肌肉痉挛，并使身体更难以自我冷却。

脱水的严重程度取决于具体情况。温格博士指出，运动中适度的液体流失是可以预期的，不一定是危险的。在健康人员运动时，身体有机制可以应对这些变化并促进液体补充。但如果液体流失持续且未得到充分补充，问题就大了。罗斯纳博士表示，严重脱水最终会影响肾脏、大脑和心血管系统。

这种测试被称为皮肤弹性测试或皮肤捏捏测试。皮肤弹性是皮肤弹性的衡量标准，这个简单的测试可以检查皮肤在轻轻捏起并放开后多久恢复正常位置。

根据美国国家医学图书馆的健康信息服务MedlinePlus，可以通过捏后背、腹部或上胸的皮肤几秒钟，然后松手来检查皮肤弹性。通常，皮肤应该迅速恢复原位。轻度脱水可能使皮肤恢复稍慢，而较差的皮肤弹性通常是中度或严重液体流失的典型表现。

尽管被称为“2秒钟测试”，但不要过于纠结于准确计时。重要的是观察松手后皮肤的行为。当身体失去足够的液体时，皮肤会失去部分正常弹性。因此，皮肤弹性是医疗专业人员评估脱水的一个身体迹象。

关于皮肤捏捏测试的发明人没有明确记载。皮肤弹性作为临床迹象已经使用了几十年，研究人员在它成为互联网健康技巧之前就开始研究皮肤弹性与脱水的关系。

国家医学图书馆索引的最早一篇论文可以追溯到1957年，当时研究人员在《儿科学》上发表了一篇研究，探讨皮肤弹性是否可以与白鼠的脱水定量关联。这项研究没有建立现代临床测试，但表明科学家们已经研究这种联系近70年了。

皮肤捏捏测试肯定不是血液检测的家用版本，但它可以是一个有用的工具。罗斯纳博士说：“这个测试只是用于确定脱水的多个快速测试之一，对年轻人最有用，但应该与其他症状和体征结合使用。”罗斯纳博士指出，这个测试在65岁以上的成年人中可靠性较低，因为皮肤会随着年龄自然失去弹性。这意味着即使没有脱水问题，某人的皮肤也可能慢慢恢复。温格博士更直白地称这个测试“极其不可靠”，指出年龄、疾病和皮肤的基本状况都会影响结果。

结论是什么？如果你感兴趣，可以尝试一下，但也要注意身体的其他信号。

脱水可以以多种方式表现出来。关键是寻找模式，而非依赖一个症状。以下是需要注意的信号：

需要注意的是，清澈的尿液并不意味着你已经达到完美的水合状态。罗斯纳博士称这是另一个误区。他说：“尿液的颜色变化很大，水合程度只是其中一个因素。”因此，如果你的尿液比平时浓一些，值得注意，但不要立刻假设脱水就是原因。

不一定。罗斯纳博士说：“口渴是脱水过程的早期信号，可以被视为身体的早期警报系统。”换句话说，口渴正在发挥它应有的作用，提醒你喝水。

温格博士解释，身体密切关注血液中液体的浓度。当你出汗流失水分时，这种浓度会升高。下丘脑会感知变化并触发激素反应，帮助肾脏保留水分。

这些调整发生在身体对整体液体容量显著下降反应之前，温格博士说：“健康成年人可以安全地依赖口渴来衡量水分需求”，但在极端高温下，制定水分补充计划可能是明智之举。罗斯纳博士也持类似观点，称口渴是“一种正常的功能性喝水信号”而非医疗紧急情况。

然而，口渴可能对所有人并不同样有效。2023年发表在《营养学》杂志上的一篇论文评述指出，老年人特别容易出现脱水，部分原因是衰老会影响控制口渴和水分平衡的系统。

因此，感到口渴时就喝水。不需要将其视为已经未能通过某种水合测试的证据。

长期摄入的水分少于流失量可能会随着时间的推移导致健康问题，但“慢性脱水”这个概念比听起来更难定义。

罗斯纳博士说：“这是有争议的，尚不清楚我们是否能定义慢性脱水。”他建议可以这样理解，即水分摄入“长时间持续低于水分流失”。可能的后果包括肾脏问题、肾结石、尿路感染、便秘、头痛、疲劳和脑雾。

在肾结石方面，证据特别令人信服。2023年发表在《营养学》杂志上的评述发现，增加水分摄入可以帮助预防首次肾结石，并降低曾患过肾结石者的复发风险。

水合状态可能影响我们的衰老过程，但相关研究仍在发展中。2023年发表在《e生物医学》上的研究分析了超过1.1万名成年人的健康数据，发现那些血清钠水平处于正常范围上限的人（研究人员将其视为水合习惯的指标）更有可能表现出加速的生物学衰老迹象，并在晚年患慢性病的风险更高。然而，美国国家卫生研究院在报道这项研究时强调，研究发现了相关性，而非证据表明更好的水合状态能减缓衰老或预防疾病。

是的，但过度纠正没有好处：水喝多了不一定更好。

罗斯纳博士说，喝太多水会稀释血液中的钠，导致低钠血症，可能会危及生命。他还说，熟悉的“每天八杯水”的规则并不适用于所有人，因为个体水分需求有所不同。

此外，水分不一定都来自杯子。罗斯纳指出，含水量高的食物，包括水果，也会增加水分摄入。

你可能认为脱水仅是热天的问题。现实是“脱水可以在任何天气中发生，只要水分流失没有得到充分补充”，温格博士说。

高温确实增加了风险。根据美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）的说法，脱水是热相关疾病的重要风险因素，长时间在高温环境中运动会导致大量汗水流失。但寒冷天气不会阻止你通过运动、疾病或日常机能流失水分。

不同的是，你可能不那么容易感觉到喝水的需求。七月的炎热天气几乎会提醒你拿起水杯。但寒冷的晨跑或意外温暖的秋日午后可能不会。因此，温度很重要，但不是决定性因素。如果你流失的水分多于补充的水分，任何季节都可能发生脱水。

温格博士说：“当脱水发展到身体无法充分向器官输送血液时，这些器官将开始显示出功能障碍。”这可能影响大脑、心脏、肾脏、肝脏、肠道等。罗斯纳博士指出，严重脱水可能导致极度嗜睡、肾衰竭、癫痫发作或低血容量休克。

到了那个程度，就别管皮肤捏捏测试了，赶紧求医。根据MedLine Plus，需要注意的症状包括混淆、晕倒、心跳加快、呼吸加快、不能排尿和休克。休克的症状可能包括苍白的皮肤、微弱的脉搏、冷手冷脚、出汗和失去知觉。

这篇文章最初发表在《读者文摘》上，标题为《这个2秒钟测试可以立即告诉你是否脱水——尤其是你还表现出这些症状时》。
articles.summary:
Dehydration is annoyingly good at disguising itself as other problems. Your head hurts, so you blame your screen. You feel wiped out, so you blame your sleep. You stand up and get a little dizzy, and your brain immediately goes somewhere more dramatic: Do I have an iron deficiency? Is my blood sugar low? Am I dying? 

Sometimes, you just need more fluids. But while it’s easy to assume everyone is walking around at least a little dehydrated, hydration isn’t that simple to measure. The good news is that your body tends to leave clues. There are the obvious ones, like thirst, but plenty of others are easy to miss.

There’s also a surprisingly simple physical check you can do using your own skin, and it takes just a few seconds. Before you try it, though, there’s an important catch: It can give you useful information, but it shouldn’t be the only thing you use to decide whether you’re dehydrated.

Ahead, Mitchell Rosner, MD, a nephrologist who specializes in fluid and electrolyte disorders, and James Winger, MD, a sports medicine physician who studies how the body manages fluids during exercise, explain exactly what’s happening to your body when it’s dehydrated—and how to spot the symptoms right away. Read on to learn more and keep your body running properly.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more health news, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

What happens to your body when it’s dehydrated?

As your body loses fluid, it has to make adjustments that affect circulation, temperature regulation and eventually organ function. Dr. Rosner says dehydration can reduce blood volume and lower blood pressure, forcing the heart to beat faster to keep blood circulating. Losing fluid and electrolytes can also contribute to muscle cramps and make it harder for the body to cool itself.

How serious that is depends heavily on the situation. Dr. Winger points out that some fluid loss during exercise is expected and should not automatically be treated as dangerous. In healthy people who are exercising, he says, the body has mechanisms designed to respond to those changes and encourage fluid replacement.

The concern is when fluid losses continue without adequate replacement. Dr. Rosner says severe dehydration can eventually affect the kidneys, brain and cardiovascular system.

What’s the 2-second test that can show you if you’re dehydrated?

It’s called the skin-turgor test or skin-pinch test. Skin turgor is basically a measure of your skin’s elasticity, and this simple test checks how quickly your skin returns to its normal position after you gently pinch and release it.

According to MedlinePlus, the consumer health-information service of the National Library of Medicine, you can check skin turgor by pinching the skin on the back of your hand, abdomen or upper chest for a few seconds and then letting go. Normally, the skin should quickly fall back into place. Mild dehydration may make the skin slightly slower to return, while poor skin turgor is more typical of moderate to severe fluid loss.

But despite the “2-second test” nickname, don’t get hung up on literally counting to two. What matters is how your skin behaves after you let go. When the body loses enough fluid, the skin can lose some of its normal elasticity. That’s why skin turgor is one physical sign health-care professionals may look at when assessing dehydration.

Who came up with the skin-pinch test?

There doesn’t appear to be one documented inventor of the skin-pinch test. Skin turgor has been used as a clinical sign for decades, and researchers were studying the relationship between skin elasticity and dehydration long before it became an internet health hack.

One early paper indexed by the National Library of Medicine dates to 1957, when researchers published a study in Pediatrics examining whether skin turgor could be quantitatively related to dehydration in rats. The study didn’t establish the modern bedside test, but it shows that scientists have been investigating the connection for nearly 70 years.

How reliable is it?

The skin-pinch test is definitely not a home version of a blood test, but it can be a useful tool. “The test is just one of many quick tests that can be used to determine dehydration,” Dr. Rosner says. “It is most useful in younger individuals but should be paired with other signs and symptoms.”

Dr. Rosner says the test becomes less reliable in adults over 65 because skin naturally loses elasticity as we age. That means someone’s skin can recoil slowly even when hydration isn’t the issue. Dr. Winger is more blunt. He calls the skin-pinch test “extremely unreliable,” noting that age, disease and the underlying condition of someone’s skin can all affect the result.

The bottom line? Try it if you’re curious, but pay attention to what else your body is telling you too.

What are the other signs of dehydration?

Dehydration can show up in multiple ways. The key is to look for a pattern instead of relying on one symptom. Here’s what to watch for:

  • Thirst: This, of course, is one of your body’s built-in signals telling you it’s time to drink.
  • Dry mouth: A dry or sticky mouth can be another clue that you need more fluids.
  • Darker urine: More concentrated urine generally looks darker, though color can also be affected by medications, vitamins (like B-complex and carotene) and other factors.
  • Urinating less often: If you’re going to the bathroom much less than usual, your body may be conserving fluid.
  • Headache: Dehydration can trigger headaches, but, of course, a headache alone can mean approximately 900 other things—which is why context matters.
  • Fatigue or trouble concentrating: Feeling unusually tired, foggy or unfocused can also show up with dehydration.
  • Dizziness: Fluid loss can affect blood volume and blood pressure, leaving you lightheaded or dizzy.
  • Rapid heartbeat, confusion or fainting: These can signal more significant dehydration and deserve immediate medical attention.

One note: Clear urine doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve achieved hydration perfection. Dr. Rosner calls that another misconception. “The color of urine is highly variable, and hydration levels are just one of these variables,” he says. So if your urine looks darker than usual, it’s worth noticing—but don’t assume dehydration is automatically the reason.

If you’re thirsty, are you already dehydrated?

Not necessarily. “Thirst kicks in early in the dehydration process and can be thought of as the body’s early warning system,” Dr. Rosner says. In other words, thirst is doing exactly what it’s supposed to do by prompting you to drink.

Dr. Winger explains that the body pays close attention to the concentration of fluid in the blood. When you sweat and lose water, that concentration rises. The hypothalamus senses the change and triggers hormonal responses that help the kidneys conserve water.

Those adjustments happen well before the body begins responding to a major drop in overall fluid volume, Dr. Winger says. “Healthy adults can safely rely on thirst to gauge their fluid needs,” he says, although in extreme heat, having a hydration plan may make sense. Dr. Rosner makes a similar point, calling thirst “a normal functional signal to drink” rather than a sign of a medical emergency.

Thirst may not work equally well for everyone, though. A 2023 review published in Nutrients found that older adults are especially vulnerable to dehydration, in part because aging can affect the systems that control thirst and fluid balance.

So when you’re thirsty, drink. You don’t need to interpret it as evidence that you’ve already failed some hydration test.

Is being chronically dehydrated a bigger problem than you may realize?

Consistently taking in less fluid than you lose may contribute to health problems over time, but “chronic dehydration” is harder to define than the phrase makes it sound.

“This is controversial, and [it’s] not clear that we can define chronic dehydration,” Dr. Rosner says. One way to think about it, he says, is when fluid intake “consistently falls short of fluid losses over an extended period of time.” Possible consequences include kidney problems, kidney stones, urinary tract infections, constipation, headaches, fatigue and brain fog.

Kidney stones are one area where the evidence is particularly convincing. A 2023 review published in Nutrients found that increasing fluid intake can help prevent a first kidney stone and reduce the risk of stones recurring in people who have already had them.

Hydration may affect how we age, but the research is evolving. In a 2023 study published in eBioMedicine, researchers analyzed health data from more than 11,000 adults and found that people with serum sodium levels toward the higher end of the normal range (which researchers used as a sign of hydration habits) were more likely to show signs of advanced biological aging and develop chronic diseases later in life. But the National Institutes of Health, which reported on the study, stressed that it found an association—not proof that better hydration slows aging or prevents disease.

Can you drink too much water?

Yes, and there’s a reason not to overcorrect: More water isn’t always better.

Dr. Rosner says drinking too much water can dilute sodium in the blood and cause hyponatremia, which can become life-threatening. He also says the familiar “eight glasses a day” rule doesn’t apply neatly to everyone because individual fluid needs vary.

Plus, not all of your fluid has to come from a glass. Rosner points out that water-rich foods, including fruits, contribute to your intake too.

What’s the biggest misconception you probably have about dehydration?

You may think that dehydration is strictly a hot-weather problem. The reality? “Dehydration can occur in any weather in which fluid losses are not adequately met with fluid replacement,” Dr. Winger says.

Heat certainly raises the stakes. According to the CDC, dehydration is an important risk factor for heat-related illness, and prolonged exercise in hot conditions can lead to substantial fluid losses through sweating. But cold weather doesn’t stop you from losing fluid through exercise, illness or everyday bodily functions.

What changes is how obvious the need to drink may feel. A scorching July day practically reminds you to reach for water. A chilly morning run or an unexpectedly warm fall afternoon may not. So temperature matters, but it isn’t the deciding factor. If you’re losing more fluid than you’re replacing, dehydration can happen in any season.

When does dehydration become serious enough to require medical attention?

“When dehydration progresses to the point that the body is not able to adequately pump enough blood to organs, those organs will start showing signs of dysfunction,” Dr. Winger says. This can affect the brain, heart, kidneys, liver, gut and more. Dr. Rosner says severe dehydration can lead to extreme sleepiness, kidney failure, seizures or low-blood-volume shock.

At that point, forget the skin-pinch test and get medical help. Signs to watch for include confusion, fainting, rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, the inability to urinate, and shock, according to MedLine Plus. Shock symptoms can include pale skin, a weak pulse, cold hands and feet, sweating and loss of consciousness.

Sources:

  • Mitchell Rosner, MD, MACP, FRCP, nephrologist with a clinical focus on fluid and electrolyte disorders; interviewed, August 2026
  • James M. Winger, MD, family- and sports-medicine physician with an interest in fluid regulation during exercise; interviewed, August 2026
  • MedlinePlus: “Skin turgor”
  • Wound Management & Prevention: “Measures of Skin Turgor in Humans: A Systematic Review of the Literature”
  • Pediatrics: “Skin turgor as a quantitative index of dehydration in rats”
  • Sports Health: “Relationships Between WUT (Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Level) Criteria and Urine Indices of Hydration Status”
  • MedlinePlus: “Urine—abnormal color”
  • Nutrients: “Hydration Status in Older Adults: Current Knowledge and Future Challenges”
  • Nutrients: “Hydration for Adult Patients with Nephrolithiasis: Specificities and Current Recommendations”
  • eBioMedicine: “Middle-age high normal serum sodium as a risk factor for accelerated biological aging, chronic diseases, and premature mortality”
  • National Institutes of Health: “Link between hydration and aging”
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: “Heat and Cold Illness in Travelers”

articles.title: Here’s What Happens to the Tennis Balls Used at the U.S. Open (There Are *Thousands* of Them!)
articles.content:
美国网球公开赛（U.S. Open）每年使用的网球数量之多令人震惊。选手们频繁更换球，数百场比赛下来，比赛后足以让狗狗们乐翻天。那么这些网球公开赛后去了哪里？2026年8月23日至9月13日，比赛将回归纽约，正是揭晓答案的好时机。

调查发现，这些网球并非比赛结束后就消失不见，而是开始了意义非凡的“第二人生”，造福社区、环境，甚至一些意想不到的受益者。了解这些故事后，你再也不会用同样的眼光看待网球了。

美国网球协会（USTA）主办的网球公开赛中，大约使用7万个网球。考虑到比赛规模，这个数字并不意外。大满贯赛事包含超过800场单打、双打、混合双打、轮椅和青少年比赛。每场比赛都需要持续供应新球，赛前每个球场都会配备足够网球。

有趣的事实：威尔逊（Wilson）已连续45年成为网球公开赛的官方用球，是职业体育史上最长的合作之一。威尔逊表示，为适应硬地球场，该球采用优质羊毛毡，提供选手在网坛最高舞台所需的速度和一致性。

网球公开赛上，网球每7局更换一次，之后每9局更换一次，遵循大满贯规则。这意味着同一个球通常仅使用30至45分钟。

为什么更换如此频繁？因为职业选手非常挑剔。每次发球、正手击球和激烈回合中，毡面变形、球压降低。这会导致球速减慢、弹跳变化，影响可预测性。新球确保每位选手面对相同条件。

普通比赛消耗6至8打球，而五盘大战可能更多。7万个网球也就不显多了。

好在这些球并非全部进入垃圾填埋场。大部分球有着出人意料的第二人生。以下是细节：

部分比赛用球以官方纪念品形式出售。球迷可以购买真正在比赛中使用过的球，获得相对实惠的大满贯纪念品。

通过USTA于2008年启动的“绿色计划”（Green Initiatives），比赛将可持续发展纳入战略。仅2025年，该计划就再利用和回收超过1.5万个网球，多数捐赠给学校、社区组织和青少年网球项目，继续在训练场上使用。

这项小变化带来巨大环境影响。网球难以生物降解，由橡胶核心和合成毡面制成，传统回收困难。全球每年产生约3.3亿个网球，丢弃后需要超过400年才能在垃圾填埋场分解。部分球交由RecycleBalls等组织，转化为体育场地材料和其他橡胶产品，减少垃圾。

部分球用于选手见面会、签名会和球迷特别活动。如果你看到职业选手练习后签名球，可能正是比赛用球。USTA还拍卖签名球等纪念品筹集善款。

没错！大部分官方比赛用球售价10至20美元，但某些球因历史意义而价值飙升。2025年9月，卡洛斯·阿尔卡拉斯在决赛击败贾尼克·西内尔的冠军球，在苏富比拍出8.89万美元的天价。

巨星签名也能增值。威廉姆斯、费德勒、纳达尔、德约科维奇等名将签名球可卖至数百甚至数千美元，尤其与经典比赛或里程碑相关时。

下次看到毡面网球，请记住：它可能远比体育用品店3美元的价值更高。
articles.summary:
If you’ve ever watched the U.S. Open, you’ve probably marveled at the sheer number of balls that get used. Players swap them out constantly, hundreds of matches are played, and by the end of the tournament, there are enough fuzzy yellow balls to make your dog’s dreams come true. But what happens to those U.S. Open tennis balls after a tournament? As the 2026 U.S. Open returns to New York from Aug. 23 through Sept. 13, it’s the perfect time to find out.

We did exactly that, and the answer is far more interesting than you’d expect. Those tennis balls don’t simply disappear after match point. They embark on a meaningful second act that’s good for communities, the environment and even a few unexpected recipients. Once you know their story, you’ll never look at a tennis ball the same way again.

Read on to discover what really happens to U.S. Open tennis balls after the tournament—and why almost none of them go to waste.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, history, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

How many tennis balls does the U.S. Open typically use?

Short answer? A lot! The U.S. Open, run by the United States Tennis Association (USTA), typically uses about 70,000 tennis balls over the course of the tournament.

That number starts to make sense when you realize just how much tennis is played. The Grand Slam features more than 800 matches across singles, doubles, mixed doubles, wheelchair and junior competitions. Every one of those matches needs a steady supply of fresh balls, and every court is stocked before play begins.

Fun fact: The official ball has been the Wilson U.S. Open Tennis Ball for more than 45 years, making it one of the longest-running equipment partnerships in professional sports. According to Wilson, the ball is specially designed for the tournament’s hard courts, with premium woven felt that delivers the speed and consistency players expect on one of tennis’ biggest stages.

How many times does a single ball get used during the tournament?

Not many. At the U.S. Open, tennis balls are replaced after the first seven games of a match. After that, they’re swapped out every nine games for brand-new ones, following official Grand Slam rules. That means the same ball is usually in play for just 30 to 45 minutes, depending on how long the games last.

Why do they get swapped out so often? Well, tennis pros are incredibly picky, and for good reason. Every serve, forehand and blistering rally causes the fuzzy felt to fluff up while the ball gradually loses pressure. As that happens, it flies slower, bounces differently and becomes less predictable. Fresh balls help ensure every player competes under the same conditions.

A typical match goes through six to eight dozen balls, though marathon five-set thrillers can burn through even more. Suddenly, 70,000 tennis balls doesn’t sound so outrageous.

What happens to U.S. Open tennis balls after they’ve been used?

Thankfully, they don’t all end up in a giant landfill. Most U.S. Open tennis balls go on to live surprisingly productive second lives. Here’s the scoop.

U.S. Open tennis balls are sold to fans

Some match-used balls are sold as official U.S. Open souvenirs. Fans can buy authentic balls that were actually used during tournament play, giving them a fun (and relatively affordable) piece of Grand Slam history.

U.S. Open tennis balls get donated and repurposed

Through the USTA’s Green Initiatives program—launched in 2008 and championed by tennis legend Billie Jean King—the tournament has made sustainability part of its game plan. In 2025 alone, the program reused and recycled more than 15,000 tennis balls, with many donated to schools, community organizations and youth tennis programs, where they continue bouncing on practice courts long after their time on the championship stage.

It’s a small change with a big environmental impact, especially since tennis balls aren’t biodegradable. They’re made from a rubber core covered in synthetic felt that’s difficult to recycle through traditional curbside programs. And with an estimated 330 million tennis balls produced worldwide each year, discarded balls can take more than 400 years to break down in a landfill. Others are sent to organizations like RecycleBalls, where they’re transformed into materials used for athletic court surfaces and other rubber products, helping keep millions of tennis balls out of landfills.

U.S. Open tennis balls become player autographs

Some tennis balls are set aside for player appearances, autograph sessions and special fan experiences. If you’ve ever seen a tennis pro sign a bright yellow ball after practice, chances are it came straight from tournament stock. The USTA also auctions signed tennis balls and other memorabilia to raise money for charity.

Are U.S. Open tennis balls worth any money?

Absolutely! While most official match-used U.S. Open tennis balls sell for a modest $10 to $20, certain balls have become prized collectibles worth hundreds, thousands or even tens of thousands of dollars. If one happens to be part of a historic moment, its value can skyrocket. Case in point: In September 2025, the tennis ball Carlos Alcaraz served on the championship point to defeat Jannik Sinner in the U.S. Open men’s final sold at Sotheby’s for a record $88,900.

Autographs don’t hurt either. Balls signed by legends like Serena Williams, Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic have sold for hundreds—and sometimes thousands—of dollars, especially if they’re tied to a memorable match or milestone.

So the next time you see a fuzzy yellow tennis ball, remember: It might end up being worth a lot more than the three bucks you’d pay for one at your local sporting-goods store.

Sources:

  • U.S. Open: “Welcome to U.S. Open 101: A USOpen.org Guide to How Tennis Works”
  • U.S. Open: “Our Courts May Be Blue, But We’re Thinking Green”
  • Associated Press: “Tennis Ball Wasteland? Game Grapples with a Fuzzy Yellow Recycling Problem”
  • Bleacher Report: “Carlos Alcaraz’s U.S. Open Final-Point Ball Sells for Record $88K at Auction After Win”

articles.title: So You Got a Bad Sunburn—Are You Doomed to Get Skin Cancer?
articles.content:
我在70年代和80年代长大，这意味着夏天我会抹满油，躺在海滩上，旁边是我的妈妈，她把一个铝箔反光罩放在下巴下面，像是在向太空发送信号。目标是先晒伤，希望几天后能神奇地变成晒伤的褐色。
通常确实如此，但只有在忍受过两天极其不舒服的疼痛之后，我的肤色才会变成番茄红，甚至无法承受T恤的重量，必须赤裸着睡觉，涂满Noxzema（那种可怕的药味！）。
今天，我们知道太阳对皮肤的伤害非常多，从皱纹和老年斑到皮肤癌。但知之更多并不能免除我们忘记重新涂防晒霜的后果。事实上，CDC最近的全国健康采访调查发现，约有8810万美国成年人在过去一年中至少晒伤一次。而皮肤癌仍然是美国最常见的癌症，每年约有500万人接受治疗。
这引发了一个问题：一次偶然的晒伤是否会在未来导致皮肤癌？这个问题在社交媒体上很流行，TikTok用户发布了他们泛红、有时甚至起泡的皮肤照片，其他用户则警告说这种晒伤是“改变人生”的，催促他们去看皮肤科医生或定期进行皮肤检查。这个趋势触及了一个真实的恐惧：如果那一次太阳下的“失误”悄悄改变了你未来的健康怎么办？如果不是，多少次晒伤才算太多？
为了得到真实的答案，我采访了两位登记上岗的皮肤科医生，了解皮肤晒伤时实际上发生了什么，一次严重的晒伤是否会改变癌症风险，以及在红肿消退后，我们是否应该改变一些行为。请继续阅读以了解更多。

**晒伤的本质**：晒伤并不是真正意义上的“外伤”，而是内部细胞已经受损后的可见反应。Dendy Engelman博士，纽约市第五大道Shafer诊所的登记上岗皮肤科医生解释道：“这是皮肤对紫外线（UV）辐射造成的损伤的炎症反应。UV辐射可以损伤皮肤细胞中的DNA，这就是为什么皮肤会变红、发热和疼痛，因为身体正在应对这种伤害。”
更令人惊讶的是，即使没有晒伤，这种损害仍然会发生。Doris Day博士，NYU Grossman医学院皮肤科荣誉临床教授直言不讳：“晒黑是损害已经发生的证据，而不是你逃脱了损害的证明。”

**晒伤的程度与风险**：并非所有晒伤都是相同的，差异不仅仅在于你有多不舒服。Day博士表示，轻度晒伤会带来红肿、发热和疼痛。而严重晒伤则伴随剧烈疼痛、显著肿胀，甚至起泡。有时还会伴随发烧、寒战、恶心或脱水等全身症状。
起泡是皮肤科医生特别关注的指标。Day博士指出，起泡意味着损伤已经超越皮肤表层，有时甚至深入上层真皮。
“这种程度的伤害会杀死更多的细胞，引发更强的炎症反应，并留下更多残留的DNA损伤，身体需要修复。”Day博士说。简单来说，晒伤越严重，皮肤在幕后进行的修复工作就越多，长期风险也越大。

**一次严重晒伤是否会导致皮肤癌**：这是每个人都想知道的问题，两位皮肤科医生的回答是：不一定，但确实增加了风险，且晒伤的时间很重要。
Engelman博士表示：“一次严重的晒伤并不意味着一定会患上皮肤癌，但它确实会增加累积的UV损伤，从而增加未来的风险。”她特别关注青少年时期的强烈间歇性UV暴露和起泡性晒伤，但她也强调，任何年龄都应该注意防晒。“无论何时，开始严格防晒都不算晚。”
Day博士给出了一个具体数字：青少年时期的一次起泡性晒伤大约会使一生中患黑色素瘤（最致命的皮肤癌）的风险增加一倍。她解释道：“此时皮肤仍在发育，免疫系统清理受损细胞的效率较低。”早期的晒伤特别重要，因为受损细胞遗留的突变有几十年的时间积累进一步的伤害。

**其他风险因素**：除了TikTok上的“改变人生”趋势，网上还有关于跳过防晒霜以更“自然”或获得足够维生素D的讨论。Engelman博士对此表示强烈反对：“我强烈建议患者不要故意暴露未受保护的皮肤以获得维生素D。我们有更安全的方式通过饮食和必要时补充剂来维持足够的维生素D水平，而不会增加皮肤老化和皮肤癌的风险。”
Day博士提供了一个实用的折中方案：可以通过短暂的、有限的未防护暴露（例如夏季几次几分钟的手臂或腿部暴露）、富含维生素D的饮食和补充剂（如果需要）来维持健康的维生素D水平。

**晒伤后的护理**：如果已经晒伤，应该先立即采取以下措施：
1. 立即到阴凉处，避免进一步暴露。
2. 用凉水冲洗，但不要用冰水。
3. 涂抹保湿剂（如纯净的芦荟凝胶）。
4. 保持水分摄入，避免脱水。
5. 避免使用炎症类药物，如阿司匹林类药物（除非医生建议）。

**长期护理**：一旦晒伤痊愈，最明智的做法是改变你的皮肤科护理方式，而不仅仅是等待它消失并继续前进。两位皮肤科医生的结论：一次严重的晒伤，即使非常严重，并不意味着一定会得皮肤癌。但这也不是无所谓的事情。这增加了累积的UV损伤，加上你的基因、病史和你曾经在太阳下度过的每一天，都会增加风险。
好消息是，昨天、上个夏天甚至1986年的晒伤并不一定会决定你的皮肤未来。你从现在开始所做的一切仍然很重要。
articles.summary:
I grew up in the ’70s and ’80s, which meant summers spent greased up in oil, lounging on the beach beside my mother, who held one of those foil-lined reflectors under her chin like she was trying to broadcast a signal to space. The goal was to burn first in the hopes that it would magically turn into a tan a few days later.

And it usually did, but only after nursing a tomato-toned burn so painful, I couldn’t stand the weight of a T-shirt on my shoulders, and had to sleep naked, slathered in Noxzema (engulfed in that awful medicinal smell!), for at least two extremely uncomfortable days.

We know so much more today about what the sun does to our skin—from wrinkling and age spots to skin cancer. But knowing better doesn’t make us immune to the downsides of a forgotten sunscreen reapplication. In fact, the CDC’s most recent National Health Interview Survey found that an estimated 88.1 million U.S. adults had at least one sunburn during the previous year. Skin cancer, meanwhile, is the most common cancer in the country, with nearly 5 million people treated for it annually.

It raises the question: Can even one accidental sunburn cause skin cancer down the line? That question is trending on social media, where TikTok users are posting photos of their reddened, sometimes blistered skin, and others are flagging the burn as “life-changing,” urging them to see a dermatologist or start getting regular skin checks. The trend taps into a real fear: What if that one “oops” in the sun is the thing that quietly changes your health down the road? And, if not, how many sunburns is one too many?

To get real answers, I talked to two board-certified dermatologists about what’s actually happening when your skin burns, whether one severe sunburn can alter your cancer risk, and what you should do differently, if anything, once the redness fades. Read on to find out.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more health, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

What happens when you get a sunburn?

A sunburn isn’t really “damage” in the sense of an outside injury—it’s a visible reaction to injury that’s already happened inside your cells. “It’s your skin’s inflammatory response to damage caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation,” explains Dendy Engelman, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Shafer Clinic Fifth Avenue in New York City. “UV exposure can damage the DNA within skin cells, which is why the skin becomes red, warm and tender as the body responds to that injury.”

Even more surprising? You don’t have to burn at all for this damage to happen. Doris Day, MD, a clinical professor in the Ronald O. Perelman Department of Dermatology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, puts it bluntly: “The tan is evidence that damage occurred, not proof that you escaped it.”

In fact, Dr. Engelman adds, “A tan is actually a sign that the skin has been exposed to UV radiation and is producing more melanin in an attempt to protect itself. So while a tan may look healthy, from a dermatologic perspective, there is no such thing as a ‘safe’ UV tan.”

What qualifies as a “bad” sunburn?

Not all sunburns are created equal, and the difference matters more than just how uncomfortable you feel. A mild burn brings redness, warmth and tenderness, says Dr. Day. “A severe one brings intense pain, significant swelling and often blisters.” Sometimes systemic symptoms like fever, chills, nausea or dehydration can occur as well.

Blistering is the line dermatologists really pay attention to. According to Dr. Day, blistering means the damage has pushed past the surface layer of skin and sometimes into the upper dermis.

“That level of injury kills more cells, triggers a stronger inflammatory cascade and leaves more residual DNA damage that the body has to try to repair,” Dr. Day says. In short, the worse the burn, the more repair work your skin is quietly doing behind the scenes—and the greater the long-term risk.

Will one really bad burn lead to skin cancer?

This is the question everyone actually wants answered, and the honest response from both dermatologists is: Not automatically, but it does raise your risk, and the timing of that burn matters quite a bit.

“One severe sunburn does not mean that someone will develop skin cancer, but it does contribute to cumulative UV damage and can increase future risk,” Dr. Engelman says. She notes that dermatologists are especially concerned about intense, intermittent UV exposure and blistering burns during childhood and adolescence, though she’s quick to add that sun damage matters at every age. “It is never too early, or too late, to become diligent about sun protection.”

Dr. Day puts a number on it: One blistering sunburn during childhood or adolescence roughly doubles a person’s lifetime risk of melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer. “The skin is still developing then, and the immune system is less efficient at cleaning up damaged cells,” she explains. Those early-in-life burns carry particular weight because the mutated cells they leave behind have decades to accumulate further hits.

That said, adult burns aren’t a free pass. Repeated burns later in life still add to your cumulative risk. So if you had one bad burn as a kid at the pool, or one accidental burn on vacation as an adult despite years of careful sun habits, it’s not a diagnosis. It’s a risk factor added to a much longer list.

So what goes into factoring the risk?

Both dermatologists describe skin-cancer risk as something built up over time, from several directions at once, rather than caused by a single afternoon. “Skin-cancer risk is typically multifactorial,” Dr. Engelman says. Here’s what dermatologists actually weigh:

  • Cumulative UV exposure over your lifetime: This is the starting point of any risk assessment, Dr. Engelman says. Total sun exposure adds up over decades, not just from any one bad day.
  • Intense, intermittent sunburns: Dr. Day notes that the sunburns from a big vacation or a single unusually long day outside are strongly linked to melanoma specifically.
  • Years of chronic, lower-level sun exposure: According to Dr. Day, this pattern is more closely tied to basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, the more common (and generally more treatable) forms of skin cancer.
  • Tanning habits, including indoor tanning: Tanning beds are particularly risky, since they deliver concentrated doses of UVA and UVB in a short window.
  • How consistently you protect your skin: Sun-protection habits, not just exposure itself, factor into the equation, Dr. Engelman says.
  • Skin type, mole count and family history: Fair skin, a lot of moles, atypical moles or a personal or family history of skin cancer all raise your baseline risk before UV exposure even enters the picture, Dr. Engelman says.
  • Pigmentation: Fair skin, freckling, red or blond hair and a first-degree relative with melanoma all raise the baseline risk, Dr. Day says. But people with darker skin tones aren’t immune either; pigment offers some protection, not full protection.

What about skipping sunscreen for vitamin D?

In addition to the “life-changing” trend on TikTok, there’s been a lot of talk online about skipping sunscreen to be more “natural” or to get enough vitamin D. Dr. Engelman doesn’t mince words on this one. “I strongly discourage patients from intentionally exposing unprotected skin to UV radiation for vitamin D,” she says. “We have much safer ways to maintain adequate vitamin D levels through diet and, when appropriate, supplementation, without increasing the risk of premature skin aging and skin cancer.”

Dr. Day offers a practical middle ground: You can maintain healthy vitamin D levels with a combination of brief, limited unprotected exposure (think a few minutes on your arms or legs, a few times a week in summer), a vitamin D–rich diet and a supplement, if needed.

Importantly, sunscreen doesn’t block vitamin D production entirely; it just cuts down the excess UV responsible for DNA damage. Both doctors recommend a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher daily, plus hats, sunglasses, protective clothing and shade as backup.

What should you do if you get a bad sunburn?

So let’s say the damage is already done. You got too much sun and you’re dealing with a real burn. Here’s what to do:

  • Get out of the sun immediately. The first priority is stopping additional UV exposure while your skin heals, Dr. Engelman says.
  • Calm down the skin. Cool compresses, cool showers or a lukewarm bath can help soothe burned skin. Dr. Day also recommends an oatmeal bath to reduce inflammation and itching.
  • Moisturize gently. Use a fragrance-free moisturizer or pure aloe to support your skin barrier as it recovers. Skip anything with alcohol, heavy fragrance or active ingredients.
  • Stay hydrated. A severe burn pulls fluid to the skin’s surface, so drink extra water, and consider an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen if you can tolerate it, Dr. Day says.
  • Leave blisters alone. Don’t pick, peel or pop them. Intact blisters act as a sterile dressing, Dr. Day notes, and popping them raises your infection risk.
  • Skip harsh products. Avoid exfoliants, retinoids and other potentially irritating skin-care ingredients until your skin has fully recovered.
  • Know when to call a doctor. Seek medical attention if the burn is widespread or severely blistered, or if you develop fever, chills, dizziness, nausea, confusion or signs of dehydration or infection.

How can you keep your skin healthy moving forward?

Once the burn has healed, the smartest move is to change how you approach your dermatology care, not just wait for it to fade and move on.

  • Tell your dermatologist. “A history of severe or blistering sunburns is something I want to know about as a dermatologist because it helps us understand a patient’s overall risk profile,” Dr. Engelman says.
  • Consider more frequent skin checks. Depending on your history and other risk factors, your dermatologist may recommend more frequent professional skin exams, often yearly or every six months, Dr. Day says.
  • Learn the ABCDE’s of melanoma. Watch for asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, a diameter larger than a pencil eraser and evolving spots. Check your own skin monthly for anything new, changing or simply different from the rest.
  • Don’t ignore anything that bleeds or won’t heal. Any lesion that bleeds, doesn’t heal or looks out of place should be evaluated promptly.
  • Get serious about daily protection. “You cannot undo past UV exposure, but you can absolutely reduce additional damage,” Dr. Engelman says. That means daily broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, protective clothing and staying in the shade whenever possible.

The bottom line from both dermatologists: One bad sunburn, even a severe one, isn’t a guarantee that you’ll get skin cancer. But it’s not nothing either. It’s a real mark against you that adds up—alongside your genetics, your history and every other sunny day you’ve ever had.

The good news is that the burn you got yesterday, last summer or back in 1986 doesn’t have to define what happens to your skin tomorrow. What you do from here still counts.

Sources:

  • Dendy Engelman, MD, board-certified dermatologist at Shafer Clinic Fifth Avenue in New York City; email interview, Aug. 11, 2026
  • Doris Day, MD, clinical professor in the Ronald O. Perelman Department of Dermatology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine; email interview, Aug. 12, 2026
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: “Prevalence and Context of Sunburn Among U.S. Adults—United States, 2024”
  • Department of Health and Human Services: “Surgeon General Call to Action to Prevent Skin Cancer: Exec Summary”

articles.title: What’s with All the “Love” in Tennis? Here’s the History Behind the Sport’s Most Confusing Terms
articles.content:
网球场上有着独特的语言体系，许多术语听起来让人困惑。比如选手可以在比分0-40时仍未赢得一分，比赛也可能因对手弃权而告终，尽管并无人离场。还有"平分到爱球"、"让分"、"零分"和"面包棍"等术语，让新手误以为身在面包店而非赛场。即使你熟悉这些词，是否曾想过它们的由来？

随着2026年美网近在眼前（粉丝周将于8月23日开启，主赛单打将于8月30日开始），正是解码这些网球术语的好时机。为此，我采访了语言专家玛莎·巴尼特，她是节目《一路与语言》的长期主持人，多年来致力于探寻我们日常使用的词汇和短语的起源。让我们拿起想象中的球拍，一起探索网球术语的奥秘。

**爱球（零分）**
当选手未得分时，比分显示的不是零分而是"爱球"。关于"爱球"的由来，说法众多。有人认为它源自法语"l'œuf"（意思是"鸡蛋"），因为零看起来像鸡蛋。巴尼特承认这是个"迷人的词源故事"，但缺乏证据支持。实际上，在法国观看网球比赛时，当地人直接用"zéro"（零）来表示。

巴尼特推测，"爱球"可能源自"为爱好而玩"的概念，即即使没有得分或金钱利益，仍继续比赛。不过，这也只是一个理论。

**15、30、40（比分）**
网球比赛中，前三分的比分为15、30、40，代替1、2、3。巴尼特表示，这一体系源自中世纪法国的早期网球版本。最初的记录显示比分为15、30、45，后来45变成了40。这个奇怪的得分体系让人困惑了几个世纪。16世纪的一位弗拉芒作家曾质疑："为什么一分射击只算一分，两分击球只算两分？"

其中一个流行的解释是得分与钟面相关：15、30、45和60分钟，代表一局结束。但巴尼特指出，这个理论存在时间顺序问题，因为带分钟指针的钟表出现较晚。另一个理论认为得分源自"手球"（jeu de paume），即选手用手击球。根据这个解释，选手在第一分后前进15英尺，第二分后再前进15英尺，第三分后前进10英尺，从而形成了15-30-40的得分规则。还有其他理论将得分与中世纪的数字惯例或场地的标记和尺寸联系起来。这种不确定性正是词源学如此迷人的原因之一。

**平分到爱球（40-40）**
当网球比赛达到40-40平分时，选手需要连续赢两分才能赢得这一局。这个术语与法语有关，"平分"源自法语"deux"（两个）。在法国网球比赛中，当比分达到40-40时，裁判会说"égalité"（平等），而非"deux"。

**满贯（四大赛冠军）**
"满贯"最初是扑克术语，指赢得一手牌中的所有把戏，最早可追溯到19世纪初。这个术语后来被体育界采用，1933年首次出现在网球界。当时，澳大利亚选手杰克·克劳福德赢得了澳网、法网和温网冠军，并计划夺取美网冠军。尽管最终失利，但在紧张感不断升级的过程中，体育记者将"满贯"术语用于网球比赛。五年后，美国选手唐·布奇成为首位在单一赛季内赢得四大赛冠军的球员。

**弃权胜（对手退赛）**
"弃权胜"一词源自赛马运动。历史上，如果只有一匹马留在比赛中，这匹马仍需"走过整个赛道才能宣告胜利"。网球比赛中，如果对手在比赛开始前退出，另一名选手将获得弃权胜并晋级，无需比赛。

**ACE（直接得分）**
"ACE"一词源自中英语时期，最初指骰子的一面或扑克牌的A。在体育界，"ACE"在19世纪引申为网球局中的得分，1871年正式记录为"无法回击的发球"。巴尼特解释道："扑克牌中的A代表最高价值，网球中的ACE也代表最强大的发球，因为对手无法回击。" 这个术语后来引申为其他领域，如"手中有ACE"、"资深记者"或"考试满分"。

**种子选手（强势球员）**
"种子"一词源自园艺。比赛组织者希望强势选手不在首轮相遇，因此将其分散在比赛抽签中。巴尼特解释道："这就像在不同的地方播种一样。" 在网球比赛中，"种子"作为动词使用，指"分散"强势选手，而非聚集。这个体育用法最早出现在1898年，而作为名词的"种子"在1931年被记录。

**让分（重新发球）**
"让分"是最常见的例子，如发球碰触球网后落在正确的发球区。选手可以再次发球。这个词有两个定义：一个来自古英语"lǣtan"（允许、许可），另一个是"阻碍、延误"。在网球比赛中，"让分"使用的是后者，即发球受阻，因此重新发球。

**零分（6-0）**
"零分"是6-0的比赛，因为零形似面包圈。如果选手以6-0、6-0输掉比赛，就被"双零分"。"面包棍"是6-1的比赛，因为1像长长的面包棍。这些是非正式术语，但它们是球迷围绕网球运动发展出的有趣语言的一部分。

**外卡（特别邀请）**
"外卡"一词源自扑克游戏，指可以代表其他牌的万能牌。网球比赛中，"外卡"指通过特殊途径进入比赛的选手，如回归冠军（如塞雷娜）、本地热门或年轻有为的选手。巴尼特解释道："如果你想让某位特别的选手参赛，但他们未通过常规途径报名，你会给他们一张外卡。"

网球术语不仅是一系列古怪有趣的词汇，更是网球运动发展的历史见证，以及语言如何旅行、变化和传承的记录。随着美网的到来，请用不同的方式倾听网球比赛的语言。

从“爱”到“平分”，每个术语都有自己的故事——它们共同构建了网球这项运动的魅力。以下是网球中最令人困惑的术语背后的历史。

网球术语的起源可以追溯到中世纪欧洲，当时的球场和规则与现代网球大不相同。当时的网球场类似于现在的实心场地，球场用绳索围绕，球手用手掌或手套击打皮球。"Love"（爱）一词最有可能源自法语"l'oeuf"（鸡蛋），形容零分时的形状。"Deuce"（平分）则源自法国的"deux"（两个），指双方得分相等时的状态。"Break"（破发）来自"break the serve"（破发），指接发球方在发球方未能得分的情况下赢得发球局。

这些术语经过几个世纪的演变，最终成为现代网球比赛的固定用语，它们的独特历史背景也让网球比赛更具文化内涵和趣味性。
articles.summary:
Play a game of tennis or simply watch a match from the stands (or your couch), and you’ll quickly discover that the sport has a language all its own—and some of it can be quite confusing.

A player can be down love-40 without romance entering the picture. A match can end in a walkover even though nobody walks anywhere. And a player can be seeded despite the distinct lack of gardening on the court. Then there are deuces, lets, bagels and breadsticks: terms that can leave newcomers wondering if they’re at a match or a bakery. Even if you’re familiar with these words, have you ever wondered why we use them—or where they came from in the first place?

With the 2026 U.S. Open just around the corner (Fan Week kicks off Aug. 23, and main-draw singles play begins Aug. 30), there’s no better time to decode some of tennis’s most head-scratching lingo.

To serve up some answers, I spoke with language expert Martha Barnette, longtime co-host of A Way with Words, who has spent years digging into the origins of the words and phrases we use every day. So grab your imaginary racket, and let’s take a swing at some tennis terminology.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more word origins, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

Love

What it means: Zero points

If a player hasn’t scored a point, their score is not zero but love. As for why zero is called love, that’s where things get murky.

You may have heard the theory that love comes from the French word l’œuf, meaning “egg,” because a zero looks like an egg. It’s an appealing story—and Barnette admits it’s “a charming, picturesque word origin.” There’s just one problem: “It’s one of those that’s almost too good to be true,” she says. “In fact, it probably is too good to be true.”

According to Barnette, “We just don’t have any evidence that love comes from the French word for egg.” In fact, if you attend a tennis match in France, she notes, “they just say zéro.” (Yep, zero.)

So where did love come from? Barnette suggests that it may have something to do with the idea of playing “for the love of the game.” In other words, playing even when you have no points or money at stake. But even that is only a theory.

15, 30, 40

What they mean: The first three point values in a standard tennis game: 15 for one point, 30 for two and 40 for three

And yes, this is probably the moment when a tennis newbie asks the obvious question: Um, why not 1, 2 and 3? Barnette says nobody has a definitive answer.

“We do know that this system goes back to very early versions of tennis in medieval France,” she says. Early records show scores of 15, 30 and 45, with 45 later becoming 40, and the strange scoring system has puzzled people for centuries. Barnette points to a 16th-century Flemish writer who questioned the practice: “Why is not one point given for one stroke and two for two strokes?”

One of the most popular explanations connects the scoring to the face of a clock: 15, 30, 45 and then 60, or game. But Barnette says etymologists have found problems with that theory. For starters, clocks displaying minutes developed relatively late compared with tennis, creating a chronology problem.

Another theory is that the unusual scoring comes from jeu de paume, an earlier French game in which players used their hands to hit the ball. According to this explanation, players moved 15 feet closer to the net after the first point, another 15 feet after the second, and 10 feet after the third—creating the 15–30–40 progression used in tennis today.

Still other theories connect the numbers to medieval numerical conventions or to the markings and dimensions of the court. That uncertainty is part of what makes etymology so fascinating. As Barnette puts it, an expert sometimes has to be “a party pooper” when a great story turns out not to be true. “People get really creative,” Barnette says. “But nobody’s come up with the real story.”

Deuce

What it means: A tie at 40–40, after which a player must win two consecutive points to win the game

Once a tennis game reaches deuce, winning one point isn’t enough. A player who wins the next point gets advantage; if that same player wins the following point, the game is over. If the opponent wins that following point, however, the score returns to deuce.

The word itself has a decidedly French connection, Barnette explains. Deuce comes from the French deux, meaning “two.” And the number makes sense: Once you’re at deuce, you need two points in a row to win the game. “If you lose that point,” Barnette adds, “then you go back.”

The terminology provides a reminder of tennis’s French roots. Early versions of the game were played in France, and the sport’s vocabulary contains plenty of French influence. Interestingly, though, a French tennis umpire doesn’t actually say deuce when the score reaches 40–40. Barnette recalls hearing égalité, meaning “equality,” at the French Open.

Grand Slam

What it means: A Grand Slam is the achievement of winning all four major tournaments—the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and U.S. Open—in the same calendar year; it can also refer to any one of those major competitions.

“Originally, Grand Slam was a card-playing term,” Barnette explains. It referred to winning all the tricks in a hand and dates to at least the early 1800s.

The phrase was eventually borrowed into sports, and tennis picked it up in 1933. That year, Australian player Jack Crawford had won the Australian and French championships and Wimbledon and was going for the U.S. title. He ultimately lost, but “while the suspense was building, sportswriters appropriated the term Grand Slam because he would be winning all the tricks, so to speak,” Barnette says.

The term stuck; five years later, American Don Budge became the first player to win all four major championships in a single calendar year. FYI: Winning four majors consecutively across two calendar years is generally called a non-calendar-year Grand Slam.

Walkover

What it means: When a player advances because an opponent withdraws before the match begins

There’s something delightfully literal about walkover, but this expression also comes from another sport.

“Walkover is borrowed from horse racing,” Barnette explains. Historically, if only one horse remained in a race, that horse still had to “walk over the entire course to claim the victory.” The term came to describe a contest won without opposition, even though the remaining competitor still had to go through the motions of completing the event.

Tennis uses the word in a similar way: If an opponent withdraws before the match begins, the other player receives a walkover and advances without playing. Barnette points out that this is part of a larger pattern in tennis vocabulary. “So many of these terms are borrowed from other sports,” she says, “or have that French influence because, of course, that’s where the early versions of tennis were played.”

Ace

What it means: A serve that lands “in” and isn’t touched by the receiver

An ace is one of the few tennis terms that seems almost perfectly suited to its meaning: It describes a serve so effective that the opponent can’t even get a racket on it.

The word ace dates to Middle English, when it referred to the one-pip (dot) side of a die and later to the playing card. Its sporting meaning developed over time; the sense of an ace as a point in racket sports dates to the 19th century, while the specific meaning of an unreturnable tennis serve appears by 1871, according to the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

“An ace in a deck of cards is the highest value, the most powerful card,” Barnette explains. In tennis, that same idea of superiority applies to the serve: An ace is the most powerful kind of shot because “it’s completely unreturnable.”

That association with excellence eventually carried into everyday English; you can have an ace up your sleeve, be an ace reporter or ace a test.

Seed

What it means: The position of a player who is ranked and placed in a tournament draw in a way designed to keep the strongest players from meeting in the earliest rounds

This tennis term comes from gardening. No, really.

Tournament organizers don’t want all the strongest players meeting in the first round and knocking each other out immediately. Instead, top players are distributed throughout the draw so they’re more likely to face one another in later rounds. “It’s figuratively scattering seeds in different places,” Barnette explains.

In tennis, seed was being used as a verb by the late 19th century, reflecting the idea of “spreading” strong players throughout a tournament draw rather than clustering them together. The sporting use dates to at least 1898, while the noun seed in this sense is documented by 1931, according to the OED.

The metaphor is a fitting one: Just as seeds are planted in different places, the tournament’s top players are strategically spread throughout the draw. If the favorites keep winning, they’ll eventually meet later in the tournament, when the stakes—and the excitement—are higher.

Note: A seed isn’t the same thing as a player’s world ranking. Rankings help determine seeding, but a tournament seed is a separate designation.

Let

What it means: A serve or point that is replayed rather than counted

The most familiar example is a serve that clips the net but still lands in the correct service box. That’s a let, and the server gets another try.

But the word has an easily overlooked history. Barnette notes that English has two definitions for let: one from the Old English lǣtan, meaning “to allow or permit,” and another meaning “to obstruct or hinder.”

“The obstructing one, as in when a serve hits the net, comes from Old English lettan, meaning ‘to hinder, delay, prevent,’” she explains. That second meaning survives in the legal phrase “without let or hindrance.”

In tennis, the idea is just as literal: The serve was hindered, so it’s replayed.

Bagel and breadstick

What they mean: A bagel is a 6–0 set; a breadstick is a 6–1 set

Finally, some tennis vocabulary that is just as silly as it sounds.

A 6–0 set is called a bagel because the zero resembles the round shape of a bagel. A bagel means a player won a set without dropping a single game. If a player loses 6–0, 6–0, they’ve been double bageled.

A 6–1 set, meanwhile, can be called a breadstick, presumably because the number one resembles the long, thin shape of that particular baked good.

These are informal terms rather than official tennis terminology, but they’re part of the playful language fans have developed around the sport.

Wild card

What it means: A tournament entry awarded to a player who wouldn’t otherwise qualify through the usual route

“In card games, a wild card, like the Joker, isn’t stuck with its ordinary value,” Barnette says. It can stand in for something else.

Tennis uses that same idea for a player who gets into a tournament outside the normal qualification process. Maybe it’s a returning champion (looking at you, Serena). Maybe it’s a hometown favorite. Maybe it’s a promising young player the tournament organizers want fans to see.

“If you have a player you really want in this tournament,” Barnette says, “and maybe they haven’t gone through all the different usual ways to get in, but there’s something special about them … then you’re gonna give them a wild card.”

The result is exactly what the phrase suggests: an unexpected element gets added to the mix.

The bottom line

Tennis vocabulary is more than a collection of strange and colorful terms. It’s a record of how the game has evolved—and how the language around it has traveled, changed and stuck.

As the U.S. Open gets underway, listen a little differently to the language of the game. From love to let to deuce, every term has a story—and together, they’re part of what makes tennis so fascinating.
